UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.:                    )
    205(d) Rate Filing: Proposal to Establish       )

                     MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER
                    OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC

          Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,

Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) respectfully moves for leave to answer and

answers comments filed in this proceeding by PJM (“PJM Answer”) and Pennsylvania Governor

Josh Shapiro (“Shapiro Answer”). 1 Constellation seeks to respond to issues raised by the Answers

to provide information that will assist in the Commission’s decision-making process as it relates to

PJM’s August 12, 2026 Proposal (“PJM Proposal,” “IRAS Proposal,” or “Proposal”).

I.        MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

          Constellation respectfully moves for leave to answer. 2 The Commission routinely grants

motions to answer for good cause. 3 Good cause exists where an answer provides information that

assists in the Commission’s decision-making process. 4              And good cause exists here, as

Constellation’s Answer clarifies important issues raised in the Answers and thereby provides

information that will assist the Commission in addressing the Proposal.


1
  Together, those two filings are referred to in this filing as “the Answers.”
2
  This motion is made under FERC Rule 212, 18 C.F.R. § 385.212.
3
  See 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.101(e), 385.213(a)(2).
4
  See, e.g., SunZia Transmission, 191 FERC ¶ 61053, at P 46 (Apr. 17, 2025); Columbia Gas Transmission, 182
FERC ¶ 61,171, at P 9 (Mar. 17, 2023).

                                                    1
 II.        ANSWER

           The Proposal exceeds the Commission’s jurisdiction. The Proposal also unlawfully

discriminates based on load size, load date, and resource vintage, and its design is unjust and

unreasonable in numerous respects.               In arguing otherwise, the Answers misunderstand the

applicable law and conveniently ignore key features of the proposed tariff. They also incorrectly

suggest that the Proposal is the only way to address issues raised by new large loads and that the

Ratepayer Protection Pledge somehow justifies violating limits set by the FPA—neither of which

is true.

           A.       The Proposal Is Outside The Scope Of The Commission’s Jurisdiction

                    1.      The Answers Incorrectly Contend That Judicial Decisions Support The
                            View That The Commission Has Jurisdiction Whenever An Action
                            Affects The Wholesale Market

           The Answers are wrong about what courts have held in defining the scope of the

Commission’s jurisdiction. The Answers’ overall import is that any effect on the wholesale market

is enough to make the Proposal jurisdictionally acceptable—a proposition that the Supreme Court

has soundly rejected.

           First, addressing Constellation’s “targeting” argument and relying heavily on FERC v. EPSA,

577 U.S. 260 (2016), PJM’s Answer contends that the question of whether an action crosses the

jurisdictional line is all about the intent behind that action, defined at a high level of generality. 5 That

is self-evidently incorrect. As EPSA explains, the Commission could not “issue[] a regulation

compelling every consumer to buy a certain amount of electricity on the retail market,” even though

“[s]uch a rule would necessarily determine the load purchased on the wholesale market too, and thus

would alter wholesale prices” 6—regardless of whether (in PJM’s words) the “justification for” that


5
    E.g., PJM Answer 19-20 (stating that whether targeting is occurring “turns on the justification for the rule”).
6
    EPSA, 577 U.S. at 280.

                                                           2
 regulation was to benefit the wholesale market in some way. 7 Were the law otherwise, the statutorily

mandated limits on the Commission’s jurisdiction would essentially cease to exist, because—given

the connection between the wholesale and retail markets—it would be easy to claim that almost any

retail-market-targeted action was ultimately intended to have some wholesale-market effect.

        In reality, the “targeting” question—which is just one of multiple relevant factors in assessing

jurisdiction, all of which point against asserting jurisdiction here 8—is a more practical one. It asks

whether “the things [the] regulation is directed at, the control of rates and facilities … , are precisely

the things over which FERC has comprehensive authority.” 9 In EPSA, the answer was yes—not

because it was possible to hypothesize some downstream wholesale-market related justification, but

because the action in question addressed only transactions on the wholesale market and the

justification for the action matched its target. 10 Here, the answer is plainly no. The Proposal is

directed at New Large Loads’ demand for power purchased at retail and seeks to control and regulate

the terms of retail sales to those loads, including through the cudgel of curtailment. The fact that the

Proposal’s ultimate goal may be to affect the wholesale market is of no moment, as EPSA makes

clear: the Commission “cannot take an action transgressing th[e] limit” on intruding on the retail

sphere “no matter how direct[] or dramatic” that action’s “impact on wholesale rates” may be. 11

        Second, citing New Jersey Board of Public Utilities v. FERC, 744 F.3d 74 (3d Cir. 2014),

PJM’s Answer contends that IRAS is jurisdictionally permissible because it prevents States’ choices

about “retail customers and retail rates” from “‘adversely affecting wholesale capacity rates.’” 12 But

9

10

 that decision does not support PJM’s position. It predates EPSA by two years, and so does not reflect

the Supreme Court’s holding that a mere effect on wholesale rates is not enough to trigger this

Commission’s statutorily defined jurisdiction. 13 And in any event, New Jersey is distinguishable

because the Commission action at issue there directly regulated the terms of capacity auctions and

did not purport to reach into the retail sphere, although it permissibly had some effects there. 14

                 2.       The Answers Conveniently Ignore The Requirement In the Proposed
                          Tariff To Curtail A Particular Category Of Retail Customers And
                          Otherwise Mischaracterize The Proposal And Protestors’ Position

        a. The Answers mischaracterize the proposed tariff and the effect on a specific class of retail

customer, identified by retail characteristics. The Answers repeatedly contend that the Proposal does

not dictate which particular retail customers will be curtailed and claim that this demonstrates that

the proposed tariff does not intrude into States’ discretion to decide which customers should be

curtailed. 15 That is incorrect. The proposed tariff language requires that Eligible New Large Loads

be curtailed, which is a means of penalizing them for not bringing their own new generation. Indeed,

PJM’s Answer admits as much when it states that “only New Large Load may be eligible to provide

IRAS.” 16 As a result, the Proposal targets and seeks to dictate the terms of retail sales as to specific

types of retail customers, identified by retail characteristics. That is a fatal jurisdictional problem—

and the Answers have no rejoinder to it.

        The express terms of the proposed tariff, which would govern if the Commission accepted

the Proposal, make that problem clear. The proposed tariff states that “Electric Distributors”

shall “execute the [PJM] Office of the Interconnection’s directives to implement Interim Resource

14
   See New Jersey, 744 F.3d at 90-91, 98 (action preventing “uneconomic offers” from “clear[ing] the auction”).
15
   E.g., Shapiro Answer 10 (stating that the Proposal “neither targets nor directs specific retail customers to be
subject to curtailment”); PJM Answer 29 (“[S]tates/RERRAs may determine which retail customers will
implement the load reduction directives.”).
16
   PJM Answer 61.

                                                        4
 Adequacy Service Actions among the Eligible New Large Loads in the Electric Distributor’s

zone/area.” 17 It states that a proposed registry that contains only information about large loads will

“inform which New Large Loads are eligible to be called on to provide” IRAS—that is, to be

curtailed. 18 And it states that compensation will be provided for those curtailed by “compensating

all Eligible New Large Loads that provided [IRAS]”—i.e., the only retail customers that “provided”

that “service.” 19 The proposed tariff language leaves no doubt that Electric Distributors would

actually violate the PJM tariff if they bypassed curtailment of Eligible New Large Loads and chose

to curtail other retail customers instead. 20

        It is no surprise that the proposed tariff reads that way, because absent that specific direction

about curtailing Eligible New Large Loads the Proposal could not function as intended. The whole

point of the Proposal is to push New Large Loads, as PJM defines that term, to bring their own new

capacity. 21 If the curtailment consequence of a New Large Load’s failure to do so could fall on

residential customers or on New Large Loads that had complied with the BYONC requirement, then

there is no reason to believe that the Proposal would incentivize New Large Loads to bring their own

new capacity—and nothing about the Proposal would help to solve the problem of system reliability

that the Answers identify as the Proposal’s raison d’être. 22

request Electric Distributors to direct that a quantity of Eligible New Large Load Amounts … be reduced in

requested to provide [IRAS] by the [PJM] Office of the Interconnection.”).

id. at 61.

                                                         5
         In ignoring that central fact about the proposed tariff, the Answers engage in a sort of shell

game. On one hand, they insist that Electric Distributors are totally free to decide which retail

customers to curtail. On the other hand, they insist that the Proposal is needed because it will work

to ensure that new large loads like data centers shoulder the burden of bringing their own new

capacity and that the burden should not fall on existing loads that have (in the Answers’ view) already

staked a claim to existing capacity. 23 But both things cannot be true at the same time. And, as the

proposed tariff language demonstrates, the first of those things is not true. Because PJM asks the

Commission to put in place a regime that disfavors and curtails the service of a specific type of retail

customer, thus affecting whether such customers receive the retail service for which they have paid

retail rates, the Commission has no jurisdiction. 24

        It is no answer to assert without explanation (as the Answers do) that, within the disfavored

group of Eligible New Large Loads, Electric Distributors can decide which particular Eligible New

Large Loads will be forced to suffer curtailment. There is no jurisdictional distinction between

regulation of a particular retail customer and regulation of a category of retail customer identified by

specific retail characteristics. 25 Any other jurisdictional rule would be irrational. If Congress’s

jurisdictional limitation could be evaded with respect to a category of, say, three or four retail

customers simply through identifying them by category rather than by name, then that limitation

would be easy to circumvent and would create precisely the overlap between state and federal

jurisdiction that Congress legislated to avoid. 26




under IRAS but no Eligible New Large Loads have yet come online. In that specific situation, the curtailment
would presumably fall on (and harm) other retail customers. See Part II.C.3, infra; N.J. BPU Answer 2-4.

24

25

         PJM’s Answer claims that the Commission’s recent decision in Tri-State Generation &

Transmission Association, 196 FERC ¶ 61,127 (2026), illustrates that “tariff provisions addressing

‘concerns regarding the rapid growth of large loads[]’ do not constitute ‘an impermissible intrusion

upon retail rate regulation’” so long as utilities have some discretion about exactly how those

provisions affect their retail customers. 27 But Tri-State does not illustrate any such thing. In an

earlier 2025 decision, the Commission rejected a prior Tri-State proposal for addressing large loads

that would have required Tri-State’s wholesale customers to set minimum load and energy

requirements for retail customers with which they dealt. 28 The Commission explained that the

proposed tariff “require[d] specific terms and conditions of service by a Utility Member to an end-

use [High Impact Load] Customer (i.e., a retail service)” and that the “specification of terms of sale

at retail ‘is a job for the States alone.’” 29 Subsequently, Tri-State revised its proposal to eliminate

any requirement that a utility take action with respect to any retail customer; the new proposal placed

requirements directly on utilities involving only “provision of transmission service and wholesale

power,” without “dictat[ing] the terms or conditions of retail service.” 30 The Commission’s 2026

decision deems that new proposal jurisdictionally acceptable because it “does not include provisions

that establish” such terms or conditions, but instead “impos[es] obligations only on Tri-State’s Utility

Members and leav[es] those same Utility Members full discretion as to whether they will flow …

through” the consequences to retail customers. 31

        The Proposal here is like the first Tri-State proposal that the Commission rejected, not like

the second Tri-State proposal that the Commission accepted. PJM’s Proposal unquestionably

   Tri-State Generation and Transmission Ass’n, 193 FERC ¶ 61,070, at PP 49-50 (2025).

 “dictate[s] the terms or conditions of retail service,” 32 because it requires that electric distributors

interrupt retail customers’ service in certain specified circumstances—indeed, PJM’s proposed tariff

requires curtailment of a certain specified category of retail customers. 33 Nothing about that 2026

decision suggests that it is jurisdictionally permissible for a tariff to regulate retail sales, let alone

categories of retail sales, so long as the tariff does not specify an individual retail customer who is to

be affected. Rather, the decision simply accepts a proposed tariff that does not establish “terms or

conditions of retail service” of any kind and leaves it entirely up to the utility whether and how the

tariff’s terms might ultimately have a trickle-down effect on retail customers. 34 Electric distributors

have no such “full discretion” 35 under PJM’s proposed tariff.

         b.   The Answers essentially admit that the Proposal’s compensation provisions are

jurisdictionally improper. As Constellation’s Protest explains, the proposed tariff’s compensation

provisions fall on the wrong side of the jurisdictional line because they effectively regulate a retail

rate by fixing the default amount that retail customers are paid for the interruption of their retail

service under IRAS. 36 The Answers respond only by asserting that the compensation provisions—

albeit “confusi[ng]” and in need of “clarifi[cation]” 37 —“target[] wholesale rates for wholesale

customers.” 38 It is difficult to see how that could be so, and the Answers do not provide any relevant

explanation. Under the proposed tariff, Eligible Large Loads would have their retail service curtailed

and would be provided compensation for that retail curtailment in their retail rates—that is, they

 would pay less because, as end-users, they received interrupted service. 39

          But even assuming that it were true that the compensation prescribed in the proposed tariff

is a “wholesale compensation level subject to change by the relevant retail authority,” 40 a fatal

jurisdictional problem remains. States can no more invade the federal government’s jurisdictional

sphere than the Commission can invade the States’ jurisdictional sphere. Thus, a retail authority

does not have the jurisdictional power to meddle in the wholesale-compensation arena by taking

responsibility for setting the level of that compensation (below a tariff-imposed cap), 41 and the

Commission cannot authorize such a jurisdictional intrusion. 42

          The Answers assert that there is precedent for giving States that kind of intrusive role: Order

No. 719, in which “the Commission granted the relevant electric retail regulatory authority (RERRA)

a veto over that existence of the wholesale [demand-response] transaction entirely.” 43 According to

the Answers, giving States the ability to reduce the amount of wholesale compensation is less

intrusive than giving them a veto, so it must be permissible. That is wrong. For one thing, as noted

above, this is a retail rate—and to say that the Commission can restrict state authority to set retail

rates is completely unprecedented.

          But even assuming that the rate here is a wholesale rate, the Answers’ argument still fails. It

is one thing (as under Order No. 719) for a federal entity with jurisdiction over the wholesale sphere

to show “solicitude” 44 by honoring the States’ desire that wholesale demand-response not take

wholesale sphere (as PJM’s Proposal does) by varying and setting the amount of wholesale

compensation. That involves the States directly reaching into and regulating the wholesale market,

which the statute does not allow. 45 If that state conduct were jurisdictionally permissible, nothing

would stop the Commission from turning over all kinds of wholesale-regulatory responsibilities to

the States—which, once again, would effectively erase the jurisdictional division that Congress

created.

        c. The Answers wrongly suggest that protestors’ position is that PJM must blind itself to

load-growth information. The Answers also incorrectly suggest that protestors’ position is that “PJM

must blind itself” to relevant data because “it is legally barred from acting on information about the

characteristics of load growth in a zone or area, even if that information is directly relevant to reliable

operation of the bulk power system.” 46 That suggestion bears no relationship to Constellation’s

actual position (or the position of other protestors). PJM is of course not barred from learning and

acting on information about load-growth characteristics. PJM can use that information to take

numerous permissible steps, including urging States to regulate retail markets differently and asking

this Commission to take actions that do not “transgress[] th[e] limit” on intruding on the retail

sphere 47—some of which Constellation identified in its Protest. 48

        But neither PJM nor the Commission is entitled to act on such information by regulating the

retail market based on the existence of certain retail characteristics, which “is a job for the States

alone.” 49 Yet that is exactly what PJM’s Proposal seeks to do. The problem is not only that “PJM

 proposes to base” the number of megawatts that must be curtailed on “whether the load growth in

[a] zone or area is comprised of new Large Loads … and whether such new Large Load additions

have been matched by addition of commensurate new supply.” 50 The problem is also (among other

things) that PJM proposes to require curtailment at the retail level “among the Eligible New Large

Loads in [an] Electric Distributor’s zone/area” 51; to dictate the default (and maximum) compensation

to be paid to curtailed retail customers in that category; and ultimately to try to strongarm New Large

Loads into obtaining retail service in a particular manner. Deeming those actions outside of the

Commission’s jurisdiction does not amount to “blind[ing]” or unduly constraining PJM.

                 3.      The Proposal Asks The Commission To Assert Authority That It Has
                         Never Asserted Before, And The Answers’ Arguments To The Contrary
                         Are Incorrect

        Finally, the Answers try to counter Constellation’s jurisdictional arguments by asserting that

IRAS involves actions “no different” from curtailment authority PJM already possesses. 52 But if

PJM already could impose the IRAS curtailment regime under existing authority, PJM’s extensive

Proposal (with its many specifications and purported justifications) would be unnecessary. Rather,

as the discussion above makes clear, the Proposal seeks to do something that has never been done

before, including choosing load to be curtailed based on specific retail characteristics of retail

customers and regulating the retail rates for such curtailment. 53 PJM’s generic authority to

coordinate emergency load shed does not involve those jurisdictionally significant features. 54

        B.      PJM’s Proposal Should Be Rejected Because It Would Violate The FPA By
                Treating Certain Load and Certain Resources Differently Without Relevant
                Justification

        Constellation’s Protest explains that PJM’s Proposal asks the Commission to unlawfully

discriminate based on load size, load date, and resource vintage. 57 The Answers concede that the

Proposal treats certain load and resources more favorably than others, yet fail to explain why that

differential treatment does not amount to “undu[e] discriminat[ion]” 58 under the FPA—including

FPA Section 202(g), which specifically prohibits undue prejudice or disadvantage in the

accommodation of anticipated capacity shortages but which the Answers never even mention. 59

                1.      The Proposal Violates The FPA By Disfavoring New Large Loads Even
                        Though They Are Not Materially Different From Other Loads

        There is no meaningful dispute that PJM’s Proposal treats New Large Loads differently—

and worse—based on their size and date of entry. 60 The Answers assert that the Proposal “neither

targets nor directs specific retail customers to be subject to curtailment.” 61 To be sure, the Proposal

does not name individual customers—but that misses the point for discrimination purposes (as for

jurisdictional ones). Under the Proposal, as PJM’s Answer expressly reaffirms, “only New Large

IRAS “is to protect native loads from the costs and reliability issues posed by New Large Loads that

        The Answers do not provide any reason why that disfavored treatment is justified by any

difference “material to the inquiry at hand.” 64 As Constellation has explained, 50 MW of demand

could come from one new customer, one existing customer, or multiple smaller new and/or existing

customers. All three scenarios place the same resource-adequacy burden on PJM, but only the first

scenario can give rise to IRAS curtailment. Although PJM suggests that New Large Loads warrant

disfavored treatment because they “have failed to cover their capacity obligations,” 65 that is exactly

the point: discrimination against New Large Loads includes not only the risk of curtailment but also

the requirement to make arrangements with new capacity, which is a burden not placed on other

customers that also impose capacity requirements.

        Indeed, PJM’s effort to justify its discrimination against New Large Loads actually confirms

that its approach is unlawful. According to PJM, “[n]ew, not existing load, is the reason for the

shortfall, which drives the need for IRAS.” 66 But the D.C. Circuit has held that “imputing an

exclusive or even primary causal role to the … demand” of the newest market entrants is not

equitable. 67 Rather, because “every shipper is economically marginal, the costs of increased demand

may equitably be attributed to every user.” 68 By contrast, PJM proposes to impose all of the burdens

        Governor Shapiro’s effort to justify discrimination against “new large computational loads”

similarly underscores, rather than refutes, the Proposal’s unlawfulness. 69 Although the Shapiro

Answer offers perfunctory statements that the loads are “new,” “distinct,” and “novel,” it does not—

and presumably cannot—explain why such loads are different with respect to their capacity needs

and resource-adequacy burdens. 70 In any event, the Shapiro Answer seeks to justify differential

treatment of computational load, but the IRAS Proposal treats all New Large Loads (including

traditional commercial and industrial load) worse than other loads. PJM has rejected the suggestion

to distinguish “data center Large Loads/computational Large Loads” from “other types of Large

Loads, such as manufacturing or industrial loads.” 71

        The Answers try to suggest that the Commission has previously approved similar

arrangements as non-discriminatory, but those analogies fail.             First, the cited decisions that

purportedly differentiated large loads from other customers are distinguishable. 72                     The

Commission’s June 2026 Order to Show Cause recognized that large customers may create

identifiable transmission and interconnection impacts—not that they pose specialized capacity or

resource-adequacy concerns. 73 And the Commission’s approval of the CHILLS proposal authorized

        Second, the cited decisions that “grandfather[] existing entities under prior rules” do not

that has always been available to all comers, creating a permanent, stark, and unfavorable difference

between otherwise identical customers.

capacity resources. 79 PJM says only that the requirement to contract with new capacity is justified

because “[t]he PJM Region needs new capacity.” 80 But that ignores that existing and new resources

can provide the very same benefit to the system, regardless of vintage. 81

         C.      PJM’s Proposal Should Be Rejected Because Its Design Is Unjust and
                Unreasonable

                1.      PJM Unreasonably Proposes to Exclude New Large Load Without
                        BYONC From the Demand Curve, Which Would Distort Market
                        Dynamics And Worsen Resource Constraints

        PJM’s proposal would unreasonably remove New Large Loads that are subject to IRAS from

the VRR Curve used to clear RPM Auctions. 85 None of the purported justifications offered in the

Answers overcomes the unreasonableness of that aspect of the Proposal.

        First, according to PJM’s Answer, its demand curve approach is justified by the Pledge. But

the Pledge is a policy statement that does not suggest that PJM’s IRAS Proposal is the only possible

approach that can be taken here, let alone that the Proposal is legally sound or is consistent with other

policies supporting new load development and infrastructure to serve that new load. 86

        Second, the Answers contend that New Large Loads that do not bring their own new capacity

should be excluded from the VRR Curve because they are “effectively electing not to receive

capacity service.” 87 But that justification makes no sense, because under the Proposal New Large

Loads without BYONC would be excluded even in delivery years when IRAS curtailment is not

triggered. 88 Similarly, in any period in which no such curtailment is taking place, the excluded load

will be physically present and served, yet the VRR Curve will pretend that it does not exist. The

categorical exclusion of certain New Large Loads from the VRR Curve thus is inconsistent with the

realities of the market, which explains why it will undermine RPM’s structural integrity and

unjustifiably mute market signals, ultimately worsening resource constraints. 89

           D.      The Answers’ Suggestion That The Proposal Is the Only Solution To The
                   Challenges Presented Is Wrong, And The Commission Should Not Be Swayed
                   By It

           Threaded through the Answers is a repeated insistence that, whatever flaws the Proposal

might have, the Commission should accept it because it is the only possible solution to an

overwhelming problem that needs to be solved this very instant. 104 That is a false construct.

           Although the Answers point to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and the Statement of

Principles (issued by the White House and Governors) as support for the IRAS imperative, those

documents contemplate solutions and responsive options for data-center demand. 105 They do not

establish that PJM’s version of IRAS is a necessary, reasonable, or lawful implementation of public

policy. Nor do they override other policy statements that emphasize the need to support “vast AI

infrastructure and the energy to power it.” 106

           Even more fundamentally, PJM’s Proposal violates the statutory limits on the Commission’s

jurisdiction—regardless of PJM’s policy motivations. Congress is empowered to decide how to

divide up responsibility for such problem-solving between the federal government and the States,

and the Commission cannot step in just because industry participants—or even States themselves—

believe that Commission action would be a more convenient or superior way of addressing a

particular issue.       Jurisdictionally improper action by this Commission is, in fact, deeply
